> **R or Rust?** The same model, functions and arguments exist in
> [R](../../r/index.html) (`verb(m, ...)` for Python's `m.verb(...)`) and
> [Rust](../../rust/basemapper_core/index.html). Coming from 0.2? See
> [Migrating to 0.3](../../migrating-to-0.3.html).

basemapper renders MapLibre GL basemaps headlessly with a Rust core: no
browser, display server, GPU or GDAL. Vector styles are drawn by a software
port of MapLibre GL JS's renderer, so maps look as they do in MapLibre.
Everything on this page was run when the page was built; the maps are the
output of the code above them.

## Installation

```sh
pip install "basemapper @ git+https://github.com/ar-puuk/basemapper#subdirectory=py-basemapper"
# or: uv add "basemapper @ git+https://github.com/ar-puuk/basemapper#subdirectory=py-basemapper"
```

See the [home page](../index.html) for conda.

## A first map

`basemap()` takes a style and what you know of the map: here a centre and a
zoom, and the image's size. In a notebook, a basemap shows the map:

```{python}
import basemapper as bm

m = bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron", center=(-111.8887, 40.7556), zoom=12.4, width=720, height=405)
m
```

Its view is a set of properties, and `provenance` says where each value came
from (*given*, or *derived* from the others, or a *default*):

```{python}
print(repr(m))
print(m.zoom, m.size, m.dpi, m.provenance)
```

The simplest style is a named basemap; `list_providers()` lists them, with
the API key some need. A MapLibre style URL or JSON works too, and so does
tile data (see [Your own tiles and services](05-own-data.qmd)).

```{python}
for p in bm.list_providers()[:8]:
    print(f"{p['name']:<24} vector={p['vector']!s:<5} raster={p['raster']!s:<5} key={p['api_key_env']}")
```

## Three controls

A map answers three questions, each with one argument:

| Question | Argument |
|---|---|
| What to show | the extent: `bounds` (an area), or `center` with `zoom` (the camera) |
| How much detail | `zoom`: which roads, places and labels the style draws |
| How sharp | `dpi`: pixels per inch (96 by default) |

`width` / `height` give the image's size, in pixels or (with `units`)
inches, cm or mm. **Any three of extent, zoom, image size and dpi give the
fourth**, and what nothing gives is defaulted: dpi 96, then 800 x 600, then
the world. The zoom is never a default; it is derived. So an area alone gets
the zoom that fits it (here North Carolina's counties, a GeoDataFrame from
[geodatasets](https://geodatasets.readthedocs.io)):

```{python}
import geopandas as gpd
import geodatasets

nc = gpd.read_file(geodatasets.get_path("geoda.sids"))
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", bounds=nc, width=720, height=300)
```

An area and a zoom give the image size: *this area at this detail*.

```{python}
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", bounds=nc, zoom=6).size
```

`around()` gives an area by its size on the ground:

```{python}
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", bounds=bm.around((-111.89, 40.76), (12, 6), units="km"), width=720, height=360)
```

And `dpi` is sharpness: the same map, with more pixels.

```{python}
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", bounds=nc, width=7, height=3, units="in", dpi=300).size   # 7 x 3 inches
```

## Renderings

`render()` draws a basemap once; the rendering converts to a PNG, an array
or an xarray, and knows where it is:

```{python}
import os, tempfile

img = m.render()
print(repr(img))
img.save(os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "slc.png"))
a = img.to_numpy()
a.shape, a.dtype
```

`m.render(dpi=192)` renders the same view at 192 dpi. `m` gives its size in
pixels, so the image keeps them and covers less ground; a basemap with no
size (or one in inches) is the same map with twice the pixels. `render_svg()`
draws an SVG, with the map as paths and the labels as editable text:

```{python}
slc = (-111.8910, 40.7608)
raster = bm.basemap("OpenStreetMap.Mapnik", center=slc, zoom=11.5, width=480, height=300)
vector = bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Bright", center=slc, zoom=11.5, width=480, height=300)

out = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for name, b in [("raster", raster), ("vector", vector)]:
    b.render().save(os.path.join(out, f"{name}.png"))
    b.render_svg(os.path.join(out, f"{name}.svg"))

for f in sorted(os.listdir(out)):
    print(f"{f:<12} {os.path.getsize(os.path.join(out, f)) // 1024} KB")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Show the four files written above.
import base64
from IPython.display import HTML

def uri(f):
    mime = "image/svg+xml" if f.endswith(".svg") else "image/png"
    return f"data:{mime};base64," + base64.b64encode(open(os.path.join(out, f), "rb").read()).decode()

HTML(f"""<table class="table" style="table-layout:fixed"><col style="width:7.5em"><col><col><tr><th></th><th>PNG</th><th>SVG</th></tr>
<tr><th>Raster<br><small>OpenStreetMap</small></th><td><img src="{uri('raster.png')}" style="width:100%"></td><td><img src="{uri('raster.svg')}" style="width:100%"></td></tr>
<tr><th>Vector<br><small>OpenFreeMap Bright</small></th><td><img src="{uri('vector.png')}" style="width:100%"></td><td><img src="{uri('vector.svg')}" style="width:100%"></td></tr></table>""")
```

## Any CRS

A map is drawn in Web Mercator, as every web map, unless it says otherwise:
`crs` gives its CRS, and a spatial layer in a projected CRS gives its own.
The map is then warped into it:

```{python}
nc_sp = nc.to_crs(32119)   # North Carolina's state plane
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", bounds=nc_sp, width=720, height=300)
```

## In a plot

`m.add_to(ax)` puts a basemap under a matplotlib axes' content. The axes
give the extent, the size and the dpi (give their CRS: plain axes carry
none); the basemap renders when the figure is drawn, lines up with the data
in any CRS, and credits the provider in the corner:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.plot(ax=ax, column="BIR74", cmap="viridis", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3, legend=True)
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

In plotnine, add it like a layer:

```{python}
from plotnine import aes, geom_map, ggplot, scale_fill_cmap, theme_void, theme

(
    ggplot(nc)
    + bm.basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")
    + geom_map(aes(fill="SID74"), alpha=0.7, color="white", size=0.2)
    + scale_fill_cmap("Blues", name="SIDS, 1974")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

[Plots with matplotlib and plotnine](03-plotting.qmd) has more.

## Clipping

`clip` draws a basemap only inside a layer's polygons; `outside()` draws it
everywhere else. An inside clip also frames the map on the layer:

```{python}
wake = nc[nc["NAME"] == "Wake"]
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", clip=wake, width=720, height=400)
```

## What basemapper tells you

Renders carry notes. A value basemapper chose is logged (the `basemapper`
logger, at INFO); something it had to change (the view kept inside the
world, an effective dpi in a plot) is a `BasemapAdjustment` warning; something
missing from the map (a tile that failed) is a `BasemapProblem` warning,
every time, and an error with `FetchOptions(on_error="fail")`.

```{python}
for n in img.notes:
    print(n.level, n.kind, n.message)
```

## The tile cache

Tiles are cached on disk, so drawing an area again does not download its
tiles again. They are kept for as long as each server allows (a day when it
says nothing), and past 250 MB the least recently used go first.

```{python}
bm.tile_cache()  # where the tiles are kept
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
bm.tile_cache(max_size=500)         # a 500 MB limit
bm.tile_cache("D:/basemap-tiles")   # another folder, for this session
bm.tile_cache(False)                # no cache, for this session
bm.tile_cache(clear=True)           # delete the cached tiles
```

To keep a folder or limit for good, set environment variables before
Python starts, for example in your shell profile:

```sh
export BASEMAPPER_CACHE_DIR=~/basemap-tiles   # Windows: setx BASEMAPPER_CACHE_DIR D:\basemap-tiles
export BASEMAPPER_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=500
```

R reads the same variables, so one folder can serve both languages.
